title: Boeing 707
wiki_lead:
The Boeing 707 is an early American long-range narrow-body airliner, the first jetliner developed and produced by Boeing Commercial Airplanes.
Developed from the Boeing 367-80 prototype, the initial 707-120 first flew on December 20, 1957. Pan Am, the launch customer, began regular service with the 707 on October 26, 1958.
With versions produced until 1979, the 707 is a swept wing quadjet with podded engines. Its larger fuselage cross-section allowed six-abreast economy seating, retained in the later 720, 727, and 737 models.
Although it was not the first commercial jetliner in service, the 707 was the first to be widespread, and is often credited with beginning the Jet Age. It dominated passenger air-transport in the 1960s, and remained common through the 1970s, on domestic, transcontinental, and transatlantic flights, as well as cargo and military applications. It established Boeing as a dominant airliner manufacturer with its 7x7 series.
The initial, 145-foot-long (44 m) 707-120 was powered by Pratt & Whitney JT3C turbojet engines.
The shortened, long-range 707-138 and the more powerful 707-220 entered service in 1959.
The longer-range, heavier 707-300/400 series has larger wings and is stretched slightly by 8 feet (2.4 m).
Powered by Pratt & Whitney JT4A turbojets, the 707-320 entered service in 1959, and the 707-420 with Rolls-Royce Conway turbofans in 1960. Also in 1960, a lighter, short-range 707-020 was introduced; it was marketed as the Boeing 720.
Powered by quieter and more fuel-efficient Pratt & Whitney JT3D turbofans, the 707-120B debuted in 1961 and the 707-320B in 1962. The 707-120B typically flew 137 passengers in two classes over 3,600 nautical miles [nmi] (6,700 km; 4,100 mi), and could accommodate 174 in one class. With 141 passengers in two classes, the 707-320/420 could fly 3,750 nmi (6,940 km; 4,320 mi) and the 707-320B up to 5,000 nmi (9,300 km; 5,800 mi). The 707-320C convertible passenger-freighter model entered service in 1963, and passenger 707s have been converted to freighter configurations. Military derivatives include the E-3 Sentry airborne reconnaissance aircraft and the C-137 Stratoliner VIP transport. In total, 856 Boeing 707s and 154 Boeing 720s were produced and delivered.

Development


Model 367-80 origins

During and after World War II, Boeing was known for  its military aircraft. The company had produced innovative and important bombers, from the B-17 Flying Fortress and B-29 Superfortress to the jet-powered B-47 Stratojet and B-52 Stratofortress, but its commercial aircraft were not as successful as those from Douglas Aircraft and other competitors. As Douglas and Lockheed dominated the postwar air transport boom, the demand for Boeing's offering, the 377 Stratocruiser, quickly faded with only 56 examples sold and no new orders as the 1940s drew to a close. grok_lead: The Boeing 707 is a narrow-body, mid- to long-range commercial jet airliner developed and manufactured by The Boeing Company, featuring a swept-wing design and four turbojet or turbofan engines. As the first successful U.S.-built commercial passenger jet, it entered service in October 1958 with Pan American World Airways, carrying up to 181 passengers at cruising speeds of around 600 mph over ranges up to 3,000 miles. With a typical length of 145 feet 1 inch and wingspan of 130 feet 10 inches, it was powered initially by four Pratt & Whitney JT3C turbojet engines each producing 13,500 pounds of thrust. Development of the 707 began in the early 1950s, stemming from Boeing's self-funded $16 million investment in the Model 367-80 prototype (known as the Dash 80), which first flew on July 15, 1954, to demonstrate jet transport feasibility. The prototype's design influenced both the commercial 707 and the military KC-135 Stratotanker, with Pan Am placing the launch order for 20 707-120 aircraft on October 13, 1955. The first production 707-120 rolled out on October 28, 1957, and made its maiden flight on December 20, 1957, achieving FAA certification on September 18, 1958. Production continued until April 30, 1991, when the 1,010th airframe rolled out of Boeing's Renton, Washington facility, encompassing commercial and military variants. The 707 family included key variants such as the initial 707-120 for short- to medium-range routes, the longer-range 707-320 introduced in 1959, and the shorter-fuselage Boeing 720 optimized for shorter flights starting in 1959. Military adaptations, like the VC-137A/B/C for presidential transport ( Air Force One from 1959 to 1990) and the E-3 Sentry AWACS surveillance aircraft first delivered in 1977, extended its legacy into defense roles. Overall, the 707 transformed global aviation by making jet travel accessible for transatlantic and transpacific routes, outselling competitors like the Douglas DC-8 and paving the way for Boeing's dominance in the jet age.
